title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1RC1LD_1LB1LE_1LE0LD_0LA0RE_1RD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1RC1LD_1LB1LE_1LE0LD_0LA0RE_1RD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The macro words and the stack structure are identified from simulation, and Lean proves the sweeps over the words; the exact rule for a round is not known yet.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 44,315 cells have been visited and 17,443 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.486). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.024).

claims.title: The sweeps
claims.text: Twenty-three shift rules over (10010)^n, (1000)^n, their rotations and three-cell words, for all n and any tapes around (one copy by rfl, all copies by TM.cross_r / TM.cross_l).

claims.title: Right-end events to 2.5·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: A C run to 5·10<sup>9</sup> steps, sampled each time the tape grows on the right (17 times): a stack of runs of d = 10010 separated by c = 1000 and a short tail; each round pushes a new top about 6 or 4/3 times the old one, the old top gains one d, and the runs below never change.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known; the exact rule for the new top is not known, so the question is not reduced to a map.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Each round this machine pushes a new, much larger block onto a stack whose lower blocks never change again, like a Collatz-like map writing down its orbit. Its exact round rule has not been found yet.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 44,315 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A stack that gains one block per round
html: Write d for 10010 and c for 1000. Each time the tape grows on the right (rarely: 17 times in 2.5·109 steps) it is a stack of runs of d separated by single c, followed by a short tail. Between these events the head sweeps over the whole tape, so the left end grows like the square root of the steps.

Each round pushes a new run at the left end, and the run that was on top gains one d; the runs below are never touched again. The new top is about 6 times or 4/3 times the old one, alternately, along with the parity of the tail: a Collatz-like map leaving a frozen record of its orbit on the tape.
The machine halts only on F reading 1, which needs A on a 1 with a 1 to its left. The exact rule for the new top is not known yet, so whether that ever happens is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.486). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.024).
After 109 steps the tape spans 44,315 cells (29,063 left of the start, 28 right), with a density of 1s of 0.394.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB1LC_1LA1LD_1LD0LC_0LE0RD_1RA1LF_1RC---: rename A→E, B→A, C→B, D→C, E→D, F→F; it is this table started in state B
  • 1RB0RA_0RC0LB_1LD1RF_1LE1RA_1RD1RB_1LA---: rename A→C, B→D, C→E, D→A, E→B, F→F and exchange left and right; it is this table started in state D, in a mirror

summary: Each round pushes a new run of 10010s about 6 or 4/3 times the previous top onto a stack that is otherwise frozen; the exact map is not yet known.
